```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 8, fig.height = 5, dpi = as.numeric(Sys.getenv("BBMM_TUTORIAL_DPI", "80")),
                      out.width = "100%")
library(Elections.BBMM)
# The long runs in this tutorial were done once (data-raw/tutorial_results.R in the
# GitHub repository) and are loaded here, so the tutorial builds in seconds.
res <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "maine_tutorial.rds", package = "Elections.BBMM"))
has_sf <- requireNamespace("sf", quietly = TRUE)
pct <- function(x, d = 0) paste0(formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = d), "%")
mins <- function(s) if (s < 90) sprintf("%.0f seconds", s) else sprintf("%.0f minutes", s / 60)
```

This tutorial fits the beta-binomial mixture model (BBMM) to the test data that ship with the
package -- Maine's 72 statewide referendums of 2008--2025 in its 462 towns -- in two ways: a fast
tempered EM fit, and the slow but fully Bayesian stepping-stone sampler. It then walks through the
posterior summaries and how to read them.

Code chunks marked **long** were run once on an Apple M4 Pro laptop (`r res$threads` threads); their
results are loaded from the package so that this document builds quickly. Running them yourself
gives the same numbers (the seeds are set), on the time scales quoted.

# 1. Installing the package and getting the test data

Install from GitHub. The package compiles C++ code, so you need a compiler: the Xcode command-line
tools on macOS (`xcode-select --install`), Rtools on Windows, or `build-essential` on Linux. Maps
also need the **sf** package.

```{r install, eval = FALSE}
install.packages(c("remotes", "sf"))
remotes::install_github("cascobayesian/Elections.BBMM", build_vignettes = TRUE)
library(Elections.BBMM)
```

The test data are part of the package: `maine` (the votes), `maine_questions` (what each question
was) and `maine_towns()` (town boundaries).

```{r data}
maine
head(maine_questions[, c("question_id", "label", "statewide_yes")])
maine$X[1:3, 1:4]   # Yes votes
maine$M[1:3, 1:4]   # Yes + No votes
```

A `bbmm_data` object is two matrices with one row per unit (here, a town or a group of towns that
report together) and one column per question: Yes votes `X` and two-option totals `M`. Blank ballots
are left out. A cell with no votes -- a question that was not on that unit's ballot -- is `NA` and
simply contributes nothing.

## Your own data

Election offices usually publish one row per unit with a Yes and a No column per question. The raw
Maine file in the repository has that layout, and `bbmm_data_from_wide()` reads it:

```{r wide, eval = FALSE}
url <- paste0("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/cascobayesian/Elections.BBMM/main/",
              "data-raw/Maine.Ref/maine_referendum_2008_2025.csv")
raw <- read.csv(url, check.names = FALSE)
names(raw)[1:5]
#> "TOWN" "REFERENDUM_2008_1_YES" "REFERENDUM_2008_1_NO" "REFERENDUM_2008_2_YES" ...
my_data <- bbmm_data_from_wide(raw, id = "TOWN", yes_suffix = "_YES", no_suffix = "_NO")
```

With two matrices of Yes counts and totals, use `bbmm_data(yes, total)` instead. Units must be
the same across all questions, so if district lines moved over the years, put every election on one
set of units first.

# 2. The model in brief

Each unit belongs to one bloc. A bloc *k* has a Yes probability $p_{kq}$ for every question *q*;
a unit in bloc *k* casts its $M_{iq}$ votes on question *q* as a beta-binomial draw with mean
$p_{kq}$ and concentration $\nu_k$, so units in a bloc scatter around the bloc's profile, more
tightly when $\nu_k$ is large. The blocs are found from all questions at once: two towns are in the
same bloc when they vote alike across the board, not on any one question.

**Tempering.** A town casts hundreds or thousands of votes on each of 72 questions, so the ordinary
likelihood treats every small, persistent difference between towns as decisive, and the number of
blocs keeps growing with the data. All three fitting methods therefore raise the likelihood to a
power $\zeta \le 1$ (the coarsened posterior of Miller and Dunson, 2019): roughly, they look for
structure that would survive if the data were a fraction $\zeta$ of their size. Smaller $\zeta$
gives fewer, broader blocs. This tutorial uses $\zeta = 0.3$ throughout. Treat $\zeta$ as a choice
about the grain of the analysis, and check that the conclusions you care about hold at neighbouring
values.

# 3. Fast: tempered EM

`bbmm_em_select()` fits the model by expectation-maximisation for each *K* in a range, from
several random starts each, holding the concentration fixed at $\nu = 100$ for every bloc.

```{r em-run, eval = FALSE}
# long: about 1 minute on 10 cores, 4 minutes on 4
sel <- bbmm_em_select(maine, K = 1:12, zeta = 0.3, n_starts = 10, seed = 2026, cores = 10)
```
```{r em-load, include = FALSE}
sel <- res$sel
```
```{r em-show}
sel
```

Each row is the best of the 10 starts at that *K*: its tempered log-likelihood, the number of
components that hold at least one town (`occupied`), the smallest bloc's share of towns, BIC, and
how many starts reached that same best fit (`n_at_best`). When few starts agree, the partition at
that *K* is one of several nearly equally good ones, and conclusions about individual small blocs
should be held loosely.

Two rules for choosing the number of blocs are reported. BIC balances fit against the number of
parameters; with tempered likelihoods it is only a heuristic. The minimum-share rule takes the
largest *K* at which every bloc still holds at least 3% (or 5%) of the units -- it stops before
the model starts carving off blocs of a handful of towns.

```{r em-plot, fig.height = 3.2}
plot_em_selection(sel)
```

On Maine the rules disagree: BIC picks `r sel$selected[["BIC"]]` blocs, the 5% rule
`r sel$selected[["min_share_5%"]]` and the 3% rule `r sel$selected[["min_share_3%"]]`. From *K* = 5 on,
fewer than half of the starts reach the best fit, and beyond *K* = 7 only one does: the extra blocs
are not well determined. We carry the 5% fit forward; the stepping-stone sampler in the next section
addresses the number of blocs directly.

Pick a fit and summarise it:

```{r em-summary}
K_em <- sel$selected[["min_share_5%"]]
fit_em <- sel$fits[[as.character(K_em)]]
s_em <- bloc_summary(fit_em, maine)
s_em
```

```{r em-map, fig.height = 7, fig.width = 7, eval = has_sf}
plot_bloc_map(s_em, maine_towns())
```

To fit a single *K*, use `bbmm_em(maine, K = 6, zeta = 0.3)`. EM also returns each town's
membership probabilities (`fit_em$gamma`); at this $\zeta$ almost all are close to 0 or 1, which
says more about the fixed-$\nu$ model than about how certain the partition is.

# 4. Slow: the stepping-stone sampler

EM gives one best partition at each *K* and no measure of uncertainty, and choosing *K* rests on
rules of thumb. The Bayesian version of the model puts priors on everything -- including a separate
concentration $\nu_k$ for each bloc -- and the stepping-stone sampler computes the **marginal
likelihood** $p(x \mid K)$ for each *K*. With a prior on *K* (geometric, favouring fewer blocs)
that gives the posterior probability of each number of blocs, and every run also leaves a weighted
sample of partitions from the posterior at its *K*.

The sampler moves a population of 200 "particles" from the prior to the tempered posterior through a
few hundred intermediate distributions, so it is far slower than EM.

> **How long will this take?** On Maine (462 towns x 72 questions), one *K* took between
> `r mins(min(res$ss_seconds))` and `r mins(max(res$ss_seconds))` on `r res$threads` threads, and
> *K* = 2 to 10 took `r mins(sum(res$ss_seconds))` in all. Time grows with units x questions and with
> *K*: a state's precincts (thousands of units) can take hours to days per *K*. Start with a small
> range of *K* around the EM answer, use as many threads as you can spare (`n_threads`), and for
> big data run each *K* as a separate job and combine them with `evidence_from_fits()`.

```{r ss-run, eval = FALSE}
# long: about 70 minutes on 10 threads (plus two extra replicates, 20 minutes)
ev <- bbmm_evidence(maine, K = 2:10, zeta = 0.3, n_threads = 10, seed = 2026)

# or, one K at a time (e.g. as separate jobs), then combine:
fits <- lapply(2:10, function(K) bbmm_ss(maine, K = K, zeta = 0.3, seed = 2026 + K, n_threads = 10))
# a second replicate at K = 6 and K = 10, to see the Monte Carlo error
reps <- lapply(c(6, 10), function(K) bbmm_ss(maine, K = K, zeta = 0.3, seed = 4026 + K, n_threads = 10))
ev <- evidence_from_fits(c(fits, reps))
ev$runs        # one row per run
```
```{r ss-load, include = FALSE}
ev <- res$ev
```
```{r ss-show}
ev
```

```{r ss-plot, fig.height = 3.2}
plot_evidence(ev)
```

Reading this output:

* `logZ` is the log marginal likelihood at each *K*, in nats (with the mean over replicates where
  there are several, and their `sd`). Differences matter, not levels: a gap of 5 nats is a factor of
  about 150 in posterior odds.
* The evidence climbs steeply up to *K* = 5 and then goes flat: from *K* = 5 to 10 the estimates
  lie within about 30 nats of each other, with no trend.
* That is the size of the Monte Carlo error. The two runs at *K* = 6 agree to
  `r sprintf("%.0f", diff(range(ev$runs$logZ[ev$runs$K == 6])))` nats, but the two at *K* = 10
  differ by `r sprintf("%.0f", diff(range(ev$runs$logZ[ev$runs$K == 10])))`. The stepping-stone
  estimate is noisy and biased low when particles lag behind, so one lucky run can take most of
  $p(K \mid x)$, as *K* = 10 does here. Do not read $p(K \mid x)$ literally when the gaps are this
  small; run replicates (`n_rep` in `bbmm_evidence()`) at the competing values.
* $p(K \mid x)$ is over mixture *components*, and components can stay empty. The robust quantity is
  $p(T \mid x)$, the posterior on the number of *occupied* blocs, averaged over *K*. Here every run
  with *K* $\ge$ 5 ends with five occupied blocs (at least 99.5% of particle weight) -- the extra
  components stay empty -- so the
  answer to "how many blocs?" at $\zeta = 0.3$ is five, whichever *K* is favoured.

Settings live in `bbmm_control()`; the defaults are the ones used here (200 particles, conditional
ESS 0.9, floor $\nu_k \ge 50$). `bbmm_rejuvenate()` enlarges a finished run's particle sample before
summarising it.

## Fixed-K MCMC

When the number of blocs is settled, `bbmm_mcmc()` samples the same posterior at that *K* with
ordinary Markov chains, each started from one of the best EM fits. It is the quickest way to put
uncertainty on one partition.

```{r mcmc-run, eval = FALSE}
# long: about 2 minutes for 4 chains x 3,000 iterations on 4 threads
mc <- bbmm_mcmc(maine, K = 5, zeta = 0.3, n_iter = 2000, n_burn = 1000, thin = 2,
                n_chains = 4, seed = 2026, n_threads = 4)
mcmc_diagnostics(mc)
plot_trace(mc)
```
```{r mcmc-plot, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 4}
plot_trace(res$mc)
```

Within a chain the traces look like stationary noise, but the chains do not all agree: the
split-$\hat R$ of the log-likelihood is `r sprintf("%.1f", res$mc_diag$rhat_ll)`, far above the
1.01 one would want.

```{r mcmc-diag}
round(res$mc_diag$mean_ll - max(res$mc_diag$mean_ll))   # mean log-likelihood per chain, vs the best
round(res$mc_diag$ari, 2)                               # agreement between final partitions
```

`r ll <- res$mc_diag$mean_ll; low <- which.min(ll); sprintf("Chain %d is stuck in a different, worse partition: its log-likelihood is about %.0f below the others, and it agrees with them only moderately (adjusted Rand %.2f--%.2f). The other chains agree with each other, and with the stepping-stone sampler's partition (adjusted Rand %.2f--%.2f).", low, mean(ll[-low]) - ll[low], min(res$mc_diag$ari[low, -low]), max(res$mc_diag$ari[low, -low]), min(res$mc_ari_ss[-low]), max(res$mc_ari_ss[-low]))`
Chain 1 is the one started from the *best* EM fit: the best partition at a single fixed $\nu$
is not the best one once each bloc has its own $\nu_k$. Each chain explores the neighbourhood of
the EM optimum it started from. Its allocation updates move
one town at a time, and at a fixed $\zeta$ on data this large the split--merge moves are almost
never accepted (`mc$acceptance` shows 0 for `split` and `merge`), so a chain that starts in a poor
mode stays there. Use `bbmm_mcmc()` to describe uncertainty around a mode, run several chains, and
always check `mcmc_diagnostics()`; finding the mode is the job of EM with many starts or of the
stepping-stone sampler, whose particles move gradually from the prior.

# 5. Posterior summaries and how to read them

`bloc_summary()` turns any fit into the same tables. For the samplers it first computes the
**posterior similarity matrix** -- for each pair of towns, the posterior probability that they are in
the same bloc -- and picks the sampled partition that agrees with it best (least-squares clustering).
Blocs are numbered by their average Yes share, highest first.

```{r ss-summary-run, eval = FALSE}
s_ss <- bloc_summary(ev, maine)   # pools the runs at every K, weighted by p(K | x)
```
```{r ss-summary-load, include = FALSE}
s_ss <- res$s_ss
```
```{r ss-summary}
s_ss
```

To see what a bloc is, start with its largest towns:

```{r bloc-towns}
a <- s_ss$assignment
votes <- rowSums(maine$M, na.rm = TRUE)
for (b in s_ss$blocs$bloc) {
  members <- a$unit[a$bloc == b]
  top <- head(members[order(-votes[members])], 8)
  cat(b, ": ", paste(maine$unit_info$name[match(top, maine$units)], collapse = ", "), "\n", sep = "")
}
```

Read together with the map and the distinctive questions below, the five Maine blocs are: (1)
Portland and its suburbs, the larger coastal towns and Bangor -- the most liberal bloc; (2) the
service-centre cities and Portland's outer suburbs (Lewiston--Auburn, Biddeford, Sanford, Augusta,
Brewer, Windham, Gorham), close to the state average on most questions; (3) Aroostook County and the
Downeast towns, a loose bloc (lowest $\nu$, lowest certainty) with its own pattern on the 2009
school-consolidation repeal, same-sex marriage and the 2024 flag question; (4) small-town and
exurban southern and central Maine; and (5) the rural interior, most opposed to the gun-safety
measures and most supportive of voter ID. These are descriptions for this tutorial, not
established names.

The columns of `s_ss$blocs`:

* `n_units`, `share`, `ballots`: how many towns, what fraction of towns, and how many two-option votes
  they cast in all. Blocs of small towns can hold many towns but few voters.
* `mean_yes`: the bloc's Yes share averaged over questions -- a rough left--right ordering, not a
  description.
* `nu`: the bloc's concentration (posterior median). Low values mean a loose bloc whose towns
  differ a good deal; high values a tight one.
* `certainty`: the average, over the bloc's towns, of their posterior probability of sharing a bloc
  with the bloc's other towns. Near 1 is a solid bloc; around 0.5 a bloc whose edges are uncertain.

## Where the blocs are

```{r map, fig.height = 7, fig.width = 7, eval = has_sf}
plot_bloc_map(s_ss, maine_towns())
```

Blocs are defined only by how towns vote, not by where they are, so geographic coherence is a
finding, not an assumption. Town-level certainty shows where the boundaries are firm:

```{r map-certainty, fig.height = 7, fig.width = 7, eval = has_sf}
plot_bloc_map(s_ss, maine_towns(), fill = "certainty")
```

`s_ss$assignment` has each town's bloc and certainty; `s_ss$membership` gives every town's average
similarity to each bloc, so for an uncertain town you can see which bloc it is torn between:

```{r membership}
a <- s_ss$assignment
uncertain <- head(a[order(a$certainty), ], 5)
cbind(uncertain, round(s_ss$membership[uncertain$unit, ], 2))
```

## What the blocs vote for

The heatmap shows each bloc's Yes share on every question (from the data, ballot-weighted). Read
across a row to see how one question divided the blocs, and down a column for a bloc's profile.

```{r profiles, fig.height = 13, fig.width = 8}
plot_bloc_profiles(s_ss)
```

Showing each bloc's gap from the state as a whole makes the distinctive questions stand out:

```{r gaps, fig.height = 13, fig.width = 8}
plot_bloc_profiles(s_ss, value = "gap")
```

`distinctive_questions()` lists them:

```{r distinctive}
distinctive_questions(s_ss, n = 3)
```

The bloc-level parameters from the model, with 90% intervals, are in `s_ss$questions`
(`p_mean`, `p_lo`, `p_hi`) next to the empirical shares (`yes_share`). The two should agree
closely; if they do not, the bloc is not well described by a single profile.

```{r questions}
head(s_ss$questions[, c("bloc", "label", "yes_share", "p_mean", "p_lo", "p_hi")])
```

**Naming blocs.** The model returns numbers, not names. Give a bloc a name only after looking at its
distinctive questions, its map, and something the votes do not contain -- demographics, partisanship,
local knowledge. Two kinds of town can vote alike for different reasons and still share a bloc.

## Questions the blocs do not explain

`question_fit()` reports, for each question, how much of the town-to-town variation in Yes share the
blocs account for (ballot-weighted $R^2$) and how far apart the blocs are. Questions near the top
divided towns along lines the blocs do not follow -- often local interests such as a casino site, a
transmission line or a school consolidation -- and are worth reading on their own.

```{r question-fit}
qf <- question_fit(s_ss, maine)
head(qf, 6)
tail(qf, 3)
```

## The shape of the blocs: Jensen--Shannon principal coordinates

`plot_js_pca()` places the towns in a space built only from their votes: the distance between two
towns sums, over questions, the Jensen--Shannon divergence between their Yes shares; principal
coordinates then find the main axes. If the blocs were slices of a single left--right dimension,
they would line up along PC1 and PC1 would carry nearly everything. Blocs that separate on PC2 or
PC3 differ in ways one ideological score misses.

```{r js-pca, fig.height = 5, fig.width = 11}
plot_js_pca(maine, s_ss)
```

Each facet title gives the share of total variation that axis carries and the share of that axis
explained by bloc membership (bloc $R^2$).

## How settled is the partition?

The posterior similarity matrix, with towns ordered by bloc, shows it directly: dark squares on the
diagonal are blocs whose towns always go together; grey bands off the diagonal are towns, or whole
blocs, that the posterior sometimes merges.

```{r psm, fig.height = 6, fig.width = 6}
plot_coclustering(s_ss)
```

## Comparing the methods

The partitions from EM, the stepping-stone sampler and MCMC can be compared with the adjusted Rand
index (1 = identical, 0 = no more agreement than chance):

```{r compare}
s_mc <- res$s_mc
c(EM_vs_SS = adjusted_rand(s_em$assignment$bloc, s_ss$assignment$bloc),
  MCMC_vs_SS = adjusted_rand(s_mc$assignment$bloc, s_ss$assignment$bloc),
  EM_vs_MCMC = adjusted_rand(s_em$assignment$bloc, s_mc$assignment$bloc))
table(SS = s_ss$assignment$bloc, MCMC = s_mc$assignment$bloc)
```

The two Bayesian methods agree closely: the MCMC's representative partition has the same five blocs,
with a handful of towns on the edges assigned differently. The EM fit (six blocs at a fixed $\nu$)
agrees less, for two reasons the cross-tabulation shows (`table(s_ss$assignment$bloc,
s_em$assignment$bloc)`): it splits the stepping-stone sampler's bloc 1 into two, and it divides the
northern and Downeast towns of bloc 3 between a bloc of their own and the small-town bloc.

# 6. Where to go next

* Fit your own data: build a `bbmm_data` object (section 1), run `bbmm_em_select()` over a broad
  range of *K*, then the stepping-stone sampler over a narrower range around the EM answer.
* Try neighbouring values of `zeta` and see which blocs persist.
* Every summary is a plain data frame, and every figure a ggplot object, so both can be extended
  with your own covariates and styling.

model. In *Bayesian Inference for Gene Expression and Proteomics*, 201--218.

Jain, S. and Neal, R. M. (2004). A split-merge Markov chain Monte Carlo procedure for the Dirichlet
process mixture model. *Journal of Computational and Graphical Statistics* 13, 158--182.

Miller, J. W. and Dunson, D. B. (2019). Robust Bayesian inference via coarsening. *Journal of the
American Statistical Association* 114, 1113--1125.
